missions.instructions: Start on the WebArena project site and navigate into its pages. Record: (1) the number of tasks in WebArena and the names of the self-hosted website categories/environments it includes (e.g., shopping, GitLab, Reddit-like forum, CMS); (2) the paper's author list and the GitHub repository link shown on the site. Then follow links to the VisualWebArena project page and record its task count, the paper authors, and the venue it was published at. Finally open the WebArena leaderboard or results page if linked and record the top reported success rate with the agent name and date. Entities: WebArena, VisualWebArena, WebArena leaderboard.
observations: Navigation traps: Redirects or URL structures (like /og/) that display content but lack standard navigation menus can trap agents.
Data ambiguity: Specific task counts are often embedded in text or sub-pages rather than prominent headers, requiring deep parsing.
Interactive elements: Elements like video sliders or shadow DOM components can clutter the DOM and make finding primary links more difficult.
Verbatim extraction: Small variations in text or dynamic loading can cause 'record_fact' tools to fail if they require exact matches.

missions.instructions: Go to the GitHub Issues page of the BrowserGym repository (ServiceNow/BrowserGym). Browse open and closed issues and record at least 5 concrete questions or problems users report (e.g., setup errors, Playwright/browser installation problems, environment registration, benchmark-specific failures for WorkArena, MiniWoB, WebArena, AssistantBench). For each, record the issue title, issue number, and the resolution or maintainer answer if one is given. Entities: BrowserGym, WorkArena, MiniWoB integration within BrowserGym.
observations: The BrowserGym domain is challenging for agents due to dependencies on specific library versions (e.g., lxml 6.0.0 causing failures), which may not be immediately obvious without deep issue browsing.
Environmental factors like headless mode and cluster-specific firewalls introduce non-deterministic failures (TimeoutErrors) that are hard for agents to diagnose independently.
Web-based benchmarks often include security features like CAPTCHAs that are intentionally designed to block or alter agent behavior, leading to 'wontfix' resolutions by maintainers.
Integration complexity between different platforms (e.g., WorkArena, MiniWoB, Google Colab) creates a fragmented setup process where errors in one component can cascade into others.
The ambiguity in user-defined custom action sets vs. default parameters requires agents to understand the underlying framework logic beyond just the surface API.

missions.instructions: Start on the GAIA benchmark dataset/leaderboard page on Hugging Face and navigate into it. Record: the number of questions in GAIA and the split between levels 1, 2, 3, the authors of the GAIA paper, and the top entries on the leaderboard (agent name and score) as visible. Then navigate to the AssistantBench project page or its Hugging Face dataset page and record its task count and authors. Then open the Online-Mind2Web or BrowseComp page (OpenAI BrowseComp announcement) and record the number of questions/tasks and the authors/organization. Entities: GAIA, AssistantBench, BrowseComp.
observations: Navigating complex web environments for benchmarking is challenging due to the dynamic nature of leaderboard data and the nested structure of information (e.g., iframes and shadow DOMs).
Verification of facts is hindered by 'quote mismatch' errors when the agent attempts to capture verbatim text that might be rendered differently or split across multiple elements.

Identifying specific authors and precise task counts requires multiple navigation steps through repository files and external paper links, which increases the likelihood of losing state or encountering anti-bot measures.

The high density of interactive elements on platforms like Hugging Face can lead to ambiguity in action targets, resulting in repetitive actions without progress if the agent's internal model of the page state is slightly off.

missions.instructions: Use the Hugging Face Papers/search interface or the arXiv listing search to explore benchmarks for web agents. On arXiv's advanced search page, search titles for 'web agent benchmark' with date filter 2024-01-01 to 2024-12-31 and sort by oldest first. Open at least 3 distinct result papers (e.g., WebVoyager, WebLINX, TravelPlanner or similar that appear) and record the exact title, arXiv ID, submission date of v1, number of authors, and the task count stated in each abstract. Do not reuse WebArena, Mind2Web, or WebShop.
observations: Navigating arXiv and its experimental HTML views can be challenging for agents due to inconsistent element IDs and overlapping text containers.
Finding specific counts (like task counts) often requires searching deep within the text or tables of a paper's HTML version rather than just the abstract.
Identifying distinct authors from lists with affiliation markers or footnotes (like equal contribution symbols) requires careful parsing to avoid including affiliations as names.
The use of 'record_fact' and 'record_source' tools in this environment is prone to 'verbatim' errors if the agent's internal text representation doesn't perfectly match the page's rendered text.

missions.instructions: Use the arXiv abstract pages for Mind2Web (arXiv 2306.06070), WebShop (arXiv 2207.01206) and MiniWoB++/World of Bits-related work reachable from the WebShop/Mind2Web pages. For each, record: the exact number of tasks/instructions/demonstrations stated in the abstract or paper, the number of websites or domains covered, the first submission date (v1), and the first and last authors. Start with the Mind2Web abstract page, then navigate to the others by their arXiv IDs (WebShop 2207.01206) and the Mind2Web paper's HTML/PDF tables for dataset comparison values.
observations: The domain of LLM web agents is characterized by a lack of standardization in task definitions, with some benchmarks using low-level instructions (MiniWoB++) while others focus on high-level, open-ended tasks (Mind2Web).
Data extraction from academic tables in HTML/PDF can be difficult due to complex layout structures and non-standardized terminology for 'tasks' vs 'environments' vs 'instructions'.

Navigating between different versions of papers (v1 vs final) and related work requires precise arXiv IDs, as title-based searches often return newer or adversarial research instead of the foundational benchmarks.
The scale of datasets (e.g., WebShop's 1.18M products vs Mind2Web's 2,000 tasks) makes manual verification of all 'tasks' impossible for a browser agent without structured comparison tables.

missions.instructions: Open the WebVoyager GitHub repository (MinorJerry/WebVoyager) and read the README and data files. Record: the number of websites included and their names (at least 5, e.g., Allrecipes, Amazon, Apple, ArXiv, GitHub, Booking, ESPN, Coursera, Cambridge Dictionary, BBC News, Google Flights, Google Map, Google Search, Huggingface, Wolfram Alpha), the number of tasks per website, total tasks, and the license. Then open the paper's arXiv page (2401.13919) and record the reported success rate of WebVoyager and the authors. Then open the WebLINX project/repo and record its number of demonstrations and websites. Entities: WebVoyager, WebLINX, Allrecipes task subset.
observations: The web agent domain is challenging due to the dynamic nature of websites (e.g., Booking, Google Flights) where data changes in real-time, making static evaluations difficult.
Navigation traps and the need for multi-modal understanding are significant hurdles, as agents must interpret visual elements and complex UI layouts to succeed.
Realistic tasks often involve long-horizon planning and handling of ambiguity in user instructions across diverse platforms like Amazon, ArXiv, and Cambridge Dictionary.

missions.instructions: Open the Hugging Face datasets listing and use its search box and filters to find web-agent benchmark datasets. Search for 'Mind2Web', then 'WebShop', then 'WebLINX' using the search field and sort by most downloads or most likes. For three distinct datasets that appear (such as osunlp/Mind2Web, McGill-NLP/WebLINX, and a WebShop-related dataset), open each dataset card and record the owner/name, number of rows or size shown in the dataset viewer, license, and the dataset's splits names. Do not use WebArena, VisualWebArena, or GAIA.
observations: Navigation traps: Searching for specific dataset names often lists models or unrelated versions first, requiring careful sorting by downloads or likes to find the canonical benchmark version.
Data structure ambiguity: Dataset split names and row counts are sometimes hidden within UI menus (like 'Subset' or 'Split' dropdowns) rather than displayed on the main landing page.
Dynamic UI: The dataset viewer often truncates content or requires horizontal scrolling to see all columns, which can obscure critical metadata like task descriptions or full action histories.
License variety: Benchmark datasets use a mix of permissive (CC-BY-4.0) and restrictive (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0) licenses, which affects their suitability for commercial training vs. academic evaluation.
Non-static values: While most metadata is stable, download counts and 'likes' change daily, making it important to focus on atomic facts like paper IDs and split names for long-term records.

missions.instructions: Go to the OSWorld GitHub repository issues page (xlang-ai/OSWorld). Browse issues and record at least 5 concrete questions users ask (e.g., VM setup, Docker, VMware/VirtualBox, evaluation reproducibility, task counts, API keys). For each, note the issue title, number, and the answer given if any. Also on the repo README, record the number of tasks in OSWorld (369) and the list of supported apps if stated. Entities: OSWorld, OSWorld-Verified, and any referenced benchmark such as WindowsAgentArena.
observations: Navigation traps: GitHub's long READMEs and pagination can cause agents to lose context or miss specific figures like task counts.
Ambiguity in 'Answers': Many user issues remain open or have partial community-driven answers that may not be officially verified.
Data volatility: Issue numbers and 'days ago' timestamps change frequently, though core benchmark facts like task count (369) remain stable.
Environment Complexity: The setup involves nested virtualization (Docker, VMware, VirtualBox), which leads to complex user queries regarding networking and port mapping.

missions.instructions: Start from the arXiv HTML version of the AgentBench paper (arXiv 2308.03688). Entities: AgentBench, WebArena-Lite or AgentBoard (arXiv 2401.13178), and GAIA (arXiv 2311.12983). Skip abstract-level claims. For AgentBench, locate the main results table and record a specific model's overall score and its score in a specific environment (e.g., Web Shopping, Web Browsing, Operating System), noting the table number. Also find the appendix with dataset statistics and record a specific number of samples or turns for one environment. For AgentBoard, find a per-task result table cell (e.g., progress rate for a named model in a named task such as WebShop or WebArena) with section context. For GAIA, find the table giving the number of questions per level or the human versus GPT-4 with plugins accuracy by level. Quote the context for each.
observations: Navigation traps: The transition between main paper text and HTML-rendered tables/appendices can cause loss of context or difficulty in locating specific cell values within large datasets.

Ambiguity in 'Specific' Requests: The prompt requires finding a 'specific model' and 'specific environment' which requires the agent to make a selection from a dense table, increasing the risk of choosing mismatched data points.
Data Density: Complex tables (like Table 2 and Table 3 in AgentBench) contain multi-layered headers (SR, Reward, F1) that are difficult to parse without a clear visual or structural map.
Fragmented Information: Facts for a single entity (e.g., AgentBench) are spread across the main results section and multiple appendices, requiring frequent internal navigation.
Verbatim Requirement: The strict requirement for verbatim quotes with context is easily tripped up by minor HTML rendering artifacts or line breaks in the source text.

missions.instructions: Start from the arXiv HTML version of the WorkArena paper (arXiv 2403.07718). Entities: WorkArena, BrowserGym, and WorkArena++ (arXiv 2407.05291). Skip abstract and README headline claims. For WorkArena, find the table of task categories and record the number of tasks in a specific category (e.g., list, form, knowledge base, service catalog, menu) and a specific agent's success rate row. For WorkArena++, find a results table or appendix describing task levels (L1, L2, L3) and record a specific count or success rate for a named model. For BrowserGym, find in its paper or ecosystem description the list of supported benchmarks and record a specific detail such as observation or action space options. Include table/section context in the quotes.
observations: The domain of benchmarking browser agents is challenging due to complex navigation structures in enterprise platforms like ServiceNow (WorkArena), which include intricate menus and forms.
Data volatility and environment state management (setup/teardown) are critical for reproducibility in web tasks.
Ambiguity in task goals and the need for multi-step reasoning (chain-of-thought) are significant hurdles for current LLMs.
Observation spaces that combine HTML, accessibility trees, and visual coordinates increase the complexity of prompt engineering and token management.

missions.instructions: Start from the arXiv HTML version of the WebArena paper. Entities for this mission: WebArena, VisualWebArena, and WebShop (cite their own papers if linked). Skip anything in the abstracts. For WebArena, find the results table comparing agents (e.g., GPT-4, GPT-3.5, text-bison) and record the exact success rate for a specific row, along with the table number and caption. Then find the appendix section listing the website categories or intent templates and record a specific count (e.g., number of templates or annotated intents per site). For VisualWebArena (arXiv 2401.13649), find a results-table row for a specific model (e.g., GPT-4V with SoM) and record the success rate per website (Classifieds, Reddit, Shopping). For WebShop (arXiv 2207.01206), find the row in the main results table for the IL+RL agent and record its score and success rate. Quote the table/section context for each fact.
observations: The exploration of the WebArena paper was partially successful, but navigation to VisualWebArena and WebShop was not completed due to termination.
WebArena's GPT-4 agent (no UA hint, CoT) achieved a 14.41% success rate as per Table 2 'End-to-end task success rate (SR %) with different prompting strategies'.
WebArena's intent distribution (Figure 6) consists of: CMS (22.4%), GitLab (22.2%), E-commerce (23.0%), Reddit (13.1%), Map (13.4%), and Cross Site (5.9%).
WebArena's Reddit-like environment includes 95 subreddits, 127,390 posts, and 661,781 users.

What makes this domain hard for a browser agent includes: 1) High sensitivity to prompt variations (e.g., UA hints), 2) Complex multi-step reasoning across diverse domains (CMS, GitLab, Maps), 3) The need for domain-specific knowledge (e.g., git merges), and 4) Fragility in action execution where small errors lead to state repetition and failure.

missions.instructions: Start from the GitHub releases page of the BrowserGym/AgentLab repository, or the ServiceNow/BrowserGym releases. Entities: BrowserGym (ServiceNow), WebArena GitHub repo (web-arena-x/webarena), and Browser Use (browser-use/browser-use). Skip README headline claims. For BrowserGym, find a specific version's release note entry and record the version number, date, and a particular change listed (e.g., added benchmark support such as WebLINX, AssistantBench, or VisualWebArena). For the WebArena repo, open the closed issues or release notes and find a specific comment inside a closed issue, such as a maintainer reply about evaluation, Docker setup, or task fixes, and record the issue number, author handle, and quote. For Browser Use, find a specific release's changelog entry (a version between v0.1.40 and v0.3) and record the version and a listed change. Include the issue/release context in each quote.
observations: Browser agents face significant navigation traps on complex platforms like GitHub where AJAX-loaded content (like release sidebars) can lead to state desynchronization between the URL and the visible UI.
Blockers include the inability to reliably extract verbatim quotes when the page structure involves nested shadow DOMs or complex text wrapping.
Ambiguity arises when multiple versions or similar sounding benchmarks (WebArena vs VisualWebArena) are mentioned across different repositories, requiring precise cross-referencing.
Data such as 'days ago' or 'latest' tags change frequently, making it hard for agents to anchor their search on static facts without specific versioning info.

missions.instructions: Start from the arXiv HTML version of the Mind2Web paper. Entities for this mission: Mind2Web, WebLINX, and MiniWoB++ (or the World of Bits paper). Skip abstract-level claims. For Mind2Web, find the results table (Cross-Task, Cross-Website, Cross-Domain splits) and record a specific cell, e.g., Element Accuracy, Step Success Rate, or Success Rate for a named baseline such as MindAct with Flan-T5-XL or GPT-4, with the table number. Also find the dataset statistics table and record the number of domains, websites, or average elements per page. For WebLINX (arXiv 2402.05930), find the appendix or dataset statistics and record a specific count such as number of demonstrations, websites, or test splits. For MiniWoB++ or World of Bits, locate a table row with a specific number of tasks or a human/baseline success rate. Include table/section context in each quote.
observations: The arXiv HTML conversion process can lead to significant accessibility and rendering issues for browser agents, such as empty initial loads or missing verbatim text during search.

Dataset statistics are often presented in complex nested tables (e.g., Table 1 in Mind2Web) where headers and data rows are separated, making it difficult for agents to associate specific values like 'Avg. # Elements' with the correct entity without persistent context tracking.

Navigation within long academic papers in HTML format requires precise scrolling and element identification, as many critical facts (like cross-domain success rates) are buried in deep sub-sections or appendices.

The dynamic nature of web-based agents means that benchmarks must account for 'real-world' website volatility, as mentioned in the Mind2Web paper's transition from simplified to real-world environments.
Mind2Web dataset statistics from Table 1: 31 domains, 137 websites, 135 average elements per page, and 2,350 tasks (noted as over 2,000 in text).
MiniWoB++ comparison statistics from Table 1: 28 average elements per page and 100 tasks (simplified mobile environment).

missions.instructions: Start from the arXiv HTML version of the OSWorld paper (arXiv 2404.07972). Entities: OSWorld, AssistantBench (arXiv 2407.15711), and BrowseComp (OpenAI paper, arXiv 2504.12516) or Online-Mind2Web (arXiv 2504.01382, 'An Illusion of Progress' paper). Skip abstract claims. For OSWorld, find the main results table and record a specific model row's success rate by category (e.g., OS, Office, Daily, Professional, Workflow) and the number of tasks in a specific application category from the appendix. For AssistantBench, find a results table row for a named system (e.g., SeeAct, SPA-ClaudeAgent) and record accuracy and answer rate. For Online-Mind2Web or BrowseComp, find a table cell for a named agent (e.g., Operator, Claude Computer Use, Browser Use) and record the score with the difficulty level or table context. Quote the table/section context each time.
observations: The domain of benchmarking LLM web agents is challenging due to the high density of tabular data in scientific papers (arXiv HTML), which often requires precise scrolling and mapping of column headers to row values across large tables.
Navigation traps include the complexity of multi-section papers where appendices contain crucial statistics not found in the main text.
Data ambiguity arises from multiple baseline configurations (e.g., A11y tree vs. Screenshot), requiring the agent to strictly maintain context of the specific model and input modality being recorded.
